title: India Posts 7.8% GDP Growth in Q1, but Data Debate Clouds the Numbers
excerpt: India's April-June growth comfortably beat forecasts, driven by an investment surge and manufacturing strength, but critics question whether a base-year revision inflated the headline figure.
body:
• India's economy grew 7.8% in the April-June quarter (Q1 FY27), beating the Reuters consensus of 7.1% and the RBI's 7% forecast.
  • Gross fixed capital formation surged 11.9% — the highest on the current data series — while personal consumption rose 7.1%.
  • Former finance secretary Subhash Chandra Garg and ex-RBI governor Raghuram Rajan questioned the methodology, citing a lower base year and a deflator well below consumer and wholesale inflation.
  • The statistics ministry defended the figures, saying a new GDP series using a 2022-23 base year and over 300 Producer Price Index deflators explains the revisions.

India's economy expanded 7.8% year-on-year in the three months through June, government data released Monday showed, comfortably beating the 7.1% growth forecast in a Reuters poll and outpacing the Reserve Bank of India's own 7% projection for the quarter.

The result marks a slowdown from the upward-revised 8.6% growth in the January-March quarter but still represents a robust start to the fiscal year, driven by a surge in capital spending and resilient consumer demand — even as the West Asia oil crisis disrupted supply chains and pushed energy costs higher.

Investment Boom Anchors the Expansion

Gross fixed capital formation — the broadest measure of investment activity — grew 11.9%, the strongest reading on the current data series. Private investment climbed nearly 12% from 5.8% a year earlier, while goods and services tax cuts and income tax reductions from earlier this year helped lift personal consumption by 7.1%.

Gross value added, which strips out indirect taxes and subsidies, grew 8.2%, suggesting underlying economic momentum remains solid. Bank credit expanded at a decade-high pace of 19% by the end of the June quarter, according to the RBI's August bulletin.

"Robust credit demand and resilient domestic consumption despite elevated prices further highlight the underlying strength of economic activity."

— Tanay Dalal, SVP Business & Economic Research, Axis Bank

Prime Minister Narendra Modi called the growth figure "a herculean feat," noting on X that "the collective strength of our people ensured India delivered such growth despite oil price shocks and supply chain issues."

A Credibility Debate Erupts

The strong headline number quickly drew scrutiny. Subhash Chandra Garg, formerly the top Finance Ministry bureaucrat, told Indian media that growth was inflated because the government had reduced its measure of GDP for the year-earlier period — the base of comparison. Under the old data series, the April-June 2025 nominal GDP stood at 86.05 trillion rupees; the new series puts it at 80 trillion rupees ($850 billion). Using the old base, nominal growth would have been just 2.6%, not the 10.3% the government reported.

Raghuram Rajan, former RBI governor, raised a different objection: if the economy is truly growing this fast, why is it not showing up in stronger job creation, domestic investment, or foreign portfolio inflows?

The opposition Congress party seized on both critiques, with general secretary Jairam Ramesh calling the 7.8% figure "statistical gymnastics." The controversy comes as Modi's government faces broader pressure after youth-led protests forced the education minister to resign in July over examination irregularities.

The Government Pushes Back

India's statistics ministry held a news conference on Wednesday to rebut the criticism. Statistics Secretary Saurabh Garg said the revisions reflect a new GDP series with a 2022-23 base year that uses more granular data sources and methodology — not any systematic bias.

"It's a combination of both these, which has led to these revisions."

— Saurabh Garg, Statistics Secretary, Government of India

The new series uses a Producer Price Index with more than 300 deflators for inputs and outputs, up from about 180 under the previous methodology. The government also adopted double deflation — separately adjusting output values and input costs for price changes — a globally accepted method.

A key point of contention is the GDP deflator, which at 2.3% sits well below retail inflation of more than 4% and wholesale inflation exceeding 9%. ICICI Securities Primary Dealership said the gap is consistent with input-cost pressures rising faster than output prices. But Societe Generale's economists said the low deflator "raises questions about the strength of real sector activity."

Mixed Signals From Other Indicators

High-frequency data broadly supports the growth story. Auto sales rose 21% in August, and net direct tax revenue climbed more than 23% year-on-year in the April-August period. But the Purchasing Managers' Index, a survey-based gauge of business activity, has weakened to multiyear lows — a divergence that adds to the debate.

For the Indian diaspora, the GDP debate matters beyond statistics. Strong growth supports the rupee and equity markets where many NRIs hold investments, while the credibility of India's economic data shapes how global investors allocate capital. The rupee has already taken the biggest hit among Asian currencies from elevated oil prices this year.

What to Watch

Economists will scrutinize the September-quarter data for signs of whether investment momentum broadens to private capex or remains anchored in government spending. The full-year growth trajectory — which some analysts estimate could reach 7.5% — will also depend on how long oil prices stay elevated and whether the monsoon season delivers relief to rural demand. For now, the debate over what India's numbers actually mean is far from settled.
